intro: A fencing mask in a museum case, a black cotton belt with a name stitched on it, a berimbau from Salvador, a banzuke printed for a sumo tournament in Tokyo and a copy of the Queensberry Rules of 1867 can all sit on the same table. Each one was made by people for a job. Each one also became evidence. Historians read these objects the way they read letters and laws: for who made them, when, where, and why they were kept.

Objects and papers do not keep themselves. Museums, archives, libraries and halls of fame choose what to save, and their choices leave gaps. Governing bodies publish rule books in new editions. Newspapers report events on deadline and sometimes get them wrong. Legends, such as the story linking Bodhidharma to Shaolin, are told beside records that can be dated, such as a stone stele carved in 728.

In this unit you will read objects as primary sources and write captions that say what an object is, where it came from and who made it. Then you will plan your own short research paper on one tradition. You will gather its founding dates, its governing body, its rule book editions and its records of who was admitted when, and you will cite each institution by name.
bigQuestion: How do objects, rule books, charters and newspapers let us tell a martial art's history truthfully, and whose story do they leave out?

timeline.t: A stele at the Shaolin Monastery records monks aiding Li Shimin
Jack Broughton publishes his boxing rules in London
Rugendas publishes prints that show capoeira in Brazil
The Queensberry Rules are published in London
Kanō Jigorō founds the Kodokan in Tokyo
Brazil's Penal Code makes capoeira a crime
The University of Chicago Press first publishes the Chicago Manual of Style
The International Fencing Federation is founded in Paris
Professional sumo begins holding six tournaments a year
The Amateur Sports Act sets up U.S. national governing bodies
The Olympic Museum opens in Lausanne, Switzerland
UNESCO adds the capoeira circle to its intangible heritage list

words.d: evidence made at the time being studied, such as a letter, photograph, newspaper or object
an object made or shaped by people and studied for what it shows about the past
the recorded history of who has owned an object, from its maker to today
museum term for a short caption giving an object's name, maker, place, date and materials
the official printed ranking list of professional sumo, issued before each tournament
a musical bow with a wooden rod, a steel wire and a gourd, which leads capoeira music
one printing of a book or rule book; later editions may change the wording
a founding document that sets up an organization and states its purpose
an organization that writes rules and runs official competitions for a sport
a traditional story told as history that cannot be proven by records
support for a claim from a second, independent record
a note that names the source of a fact so a reader can find it

test.q: Which of these is a primary source?
choices: a judo belt worn in the 1930s
test.why: An object made and used at the time is a primary source.

test.q: What does a credit line on a museum caption tell you?
choices: how the museum got the object
test.why: The credit line says whether the object was a gift, a purchase or came another way.

test.q: Which group adopted a Code of Ethics for Museums in 1986?
test.why: The International Council of Museums adopted its code in 1986 and revised it in 2004.
The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913.

test.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules of 1867?
test.why: Chambers wrote them, and they were issued under the Marquess of Queensberry's name.

test.q: What did Kanō Jigorō borrow from the game of go?
test.why: Go ranked players by dan, and Kanō adapted the idea in 1883.

test.q: Who writes the sumo banzuke by hand?
test.why: Senior gyōji write the banzuke in the sumō-ji brush style.

test.q: What law made capoeira a crime in Brazil?
test.why: The Penal Code of 1890 criminalized capoeira; the Golden Law of 1888 had ended slavery.

test.q: What is the difference between a museum and a hall of fame?
choices: a museum keeps and shows objects; a hall of fame honors people chosen by vote
a hall of fame keeps only rule books
a museum honors only living people
test.why: Museums collect objects, while halls of fame honor voted inductees.

test.q: Why should a research paper give the year of a rule book's edition?
test.why: Governing bodies revise rules, so the edition year shows which wording was used.

test.q: When did women's judo become an Olympic medal event?
test.why: It was a demonstration event in 1988 and a medal event in 1992.

test.q: What does the Shaolin stele dated 728 provide?
choices: dated evidence that monks aided Li Shimin
test.why: The stele records monks helping the future Tang emperor, which is real evidence, unlike the Bodhidharma legend.

choices: support from a second, independent record
test.why: Corroboration checks a claim against another record.

test.q: Who became the first Black world heavyweight boxing champion, in 1908?
test.why: Jack Johnson defeated Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908.

test.q: Which guide to citing sources was first published in Chicago in 1906?
test.why: The University of Chicago Press first published the Chicago Manual of Style in 1906.

write.prompt: Choose one tradition from this unit, such as judo, capoeira, sumo, fencing or boxing. What do its objects and records show about who was let in, and when? Cite two or three dated records by name, such as the Queensberry Rules (1867), the Penal Code of 1890, a banzuke, or the Kodokan's 1926 women's section.
tips: Name each record and give its date and the institution that made it.
Label any legend as a legend and set it beside a dated record.
Say which governing body you mean each time you name a rule.
Mark any fact that only one source gives as uncertain.
Use unit words such as provenance, edition, charter and corroboration.
